baer-heitev.1#א: "For example." And the same applies to cheese of a non-Jew and the like; even an issur that has a Torah root — so too the Rashba.
baer-heitev.1#ב: "Greater." The Nekudat HaKesef wrote that it is possible regarding stringent issurei mashahu we do not say "I say," even for d'rabbanan issurim with less than a majority. And the Peri Chadash disagrees.
baer-heitev.1#ג: "The pieces." The Shach wrote that even if the pieces are worthy of honor, for that too is only d'rabbanan; and the same applies to two pieces and two pots, or two pieces and one pot — it is also permitted even for a piece worthy of honor, for nevertheless it is a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient. It also appears that here it deals with when the two pieces were recognizable by themselves before they fell which was heter and which was issur; but if they became mixed first one with one, then since issur was established in both pieces each one is judged as the substance of issur itself and we no longer say a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, as written in the laws of double doubt, seif 41; and the Peri Chadash disagrees.
baer-heitev.1#ד: "D'rabbanan." The Taz wrote that it appears one should challenge what is written in this siman, that if there is a doubt whether d'oraisa issur fell, it is permitted at a d'rabbanan measure — and this contradicts the rule stated in siman 66, seif 4, that in this we do not rule leniently but it is like certain d'oraisa; and it requires further study, for here the heter is by force of "I say" that no issur fell at all — this is more lenient.
baer-heitev.2#_: "But." The Shach wrote that this deals only with two pots; but with two pieces and one pot, even if the issur pieces are greater than the pot it is permitted. And one may say: with one piece and two pots, where is this found that the issur is greater than the heter? If we know the issur is the majority we examine the pot of heter — one may say it is found well when the issur was removed beforehand (and in Nachalat Binyamin he resolved another matter, see there). However, the Raah disagrees and holds that even with two pots it is permitted even if the issur is greater than the heter, because of a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, see there, end of his words (and the Taz reconciles another matter).
baer-heitev.3#_: "That it be nullified." Meaning, in species in its species specifically a majority alone suffices, as below, seif 4. Shach.
baer-heitev.4#א: "In its species." The Taz wrote that the same applies to species in its species and not its species — for we say that what is not its species is as if it is not there, and its species is greater than it and nullifies it (as above, siman 98).
baer-heitev.4#ב: "Sixty." This deals with a piece worthy of honor, for d'rabbanan sixty does not help; nevertheless here in doubt they were lenient. Taz.
baer-heitev.5#א: "Both of them." The reason: since you forbid in any case one of them — on what basis did you forbid this one, lest the opposite — and therefore both are forbidden [Rashba]; and see below, siman 129, Semag. And accordingly it appears explicitly that even with two pots of heter that are not equal but one is small and one large, we cannot permit the large one and say the issur fell into the small one. Shach.
baer-heitev.5#ב: "Permitted." The Tur wrote that there is no distinction whether the two pots belong to one person or two people; and the Bach challenged why we do not say that the two pots combine to nullify when they belong to one person, as below, end of seif 7. And the Shach resolved that here it does not deal at all with the law of combination (tziruf); and it is possible that here it deals with those cases in which combination below does not help. He also wrote that it appears to me the main view follows the Ramban, that when belonging to two people and they come to ask about this one after the other, we suspend judgment to be lenient even if neither has enough to nullify — and all this is specifically for d'rabbanan issur; but for d'oraisa issur we do not say "I say," for a d'oraisa doubt is stringent.
baer-heitev.6#א: "The second." The Bach wrote that here it teaches that even for d'oraisa issur it is permitted; and the Taz and Shach challenged him, for this is a great principle that we do not say "I say" for d'oraisa issur.
baer-heitev.6#ב: "Forbidden." And we do not say that to the place where the last issur fell the first also fell; rather its law is as if issur fell and it is not known where it fell. Shach.
baer-heitev.7#א: "Combine." The Shach wrote that in Issur VeHeter he wrote one resolution: specifically when neither alone has enough to nullify it, only in both together; but if one has enough to nullify and the second does not, we do not say in this that it is permitted because it entered doubt — for that one which has enough to nullify did not enter doubt at all. And it appears clear that even according to what we establish chein nafsho for all issurim, nevertheless they combine, for we say chein nafsho only where it is known where it fell; but here where we do not know, we say we view them as if they were mixed at the outset at the time of falling and everything entered doubt, end of his words.
baer-heitev.7#ב: "Will become mixed." The Taz and Shach wrote, and it appears that even for one person, if it is known clearly that they will not become mixed — for example, one of meat and the second of milk, or one has something sweet and the second something pickled like vinegar, or the like — they do not combine.
baer-heitev.7#ג: "To permit." The Taz wrote, and these are his words: it appears to me astonishing at this ruling that whatever entered doubt combines to nullify it — why did he rule above, siman 105, seif 15, that if it is not known whether he touched all of them all are forbidden; why do we not say that all combine to nullify?
baer-heitev.7#ד: "That he mix them." And the Taz disagrees on this and rules that even if they were not mixed, since by Torah law it is permitted through nullification in the majority but d'rabbanan requires sixty, and since there is doubt into which it fell and both entered doubt — both combine to nullify and each is permitted by itself, since they will become mixed we view them as if already mixed, end of his words (and see siman 23).

beer-hagolah.1#_: Tur in the name of Semak, from the baraita of two pots, one of terumah, etc. — Pesachim daf 9 and daf 44 and Yevamot daf 82, and as explained there.
beer-hagolah.3#_: There, from the mishnah of two baskets, chapter 7 of Terumot, mishnah 5.
beer-hagolah.4#_: There, from the implication of the Gemara, Yevamot daf 22, from that which it challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a mikveh that has forty se'ah in it, etc.
beer-hagolah.5#_: There, in Pesachim and in the other place.
beer-hagolah.6#_: Also from that in Pesachim above.
beer-hagolah.7#_: There, and according to Rabbeinu Tam, as I cited above in siman 98, seif 2.

beur-hagra.1#א: "If the piece, etc." As written regarding two spice-measures in chapter 3 of Pesachim (44a), and chapter 6 of Nazir regarding terumat tavlin that is d'rabbanan, and regarding two baskets there and there, and chapter 1 of Pesachim regarding terumah in the present era that is d'rabbanan.
beur-hagra.1#ב: "For example, its fat, etc." Chapter gid hanasheh, 92b.
beur-hagra.1#ג: "And even if, etc." Chapter ha'Areil (2a), according to Rabbi Yochanan.
beur-hagra.1#ד: "And the same law if, etc." Tosefta end of chapter 8 of Terumot, and there all three cases: Before him were two pots, one of terumah and one of hullin, and before him one spice-measure of terumah; he put it into one of them and it is not known into which he put it — I say he put it into the terumah. Before him were two spice-measures, one of hullin and one of terumah, and before him one pot of hullin; he put from one of them and it is not known from which he put — I say from the hullin. Before him were two pots, one of hullin and one of terumah, and before him two spice-measures, one of hullin and one of terumah; he put from both and does not know whether from this into that or from that into this — I say terumah into terumah and hullin into hullin. And if it was tevel and first tithe and second tithe — it is forbidden, for they permitted doubt of dimu'a only in something that has a permitted aspect; meaning, specifically we suspend terumah into terumah; but if one was tevel and one hullin we do not suspend that terumah fell into tevel, for we suspend only where it does not forbid at all.
beur-hagra.1#ה: "Or if, etc." Mishnah chapter 4 of Terumot and that Tosefta and in chapter 6 there.
beur-hagra.2#_: "In what case is this stated, etc." Chapter ha'Areil (2b), and Rabbi Yochanan's view in d'rabbanan, etc. — not as those who disagree.
beur-hagra.3#_: "If the issur was, etc." Chapter 1 (9b), and chapter 3 of Pesachim and chapter 6 of Nazir.
beur-hagra.4#א: "If the heter was, etc." Yevamot there, and Rabbi Yochanan's view, etc., and Rabbi Yehoshua even though, etc.
beur-hagra.4#ב: "How so, etc." Even though it is d'oraisa, since the measure is d'rabbanan, as written in chapter 3 of Pesachim and chapter 6 of Nazir — it challenged him with two spice-measures, etc.; and if you say, etc., it challenged him, etc. — thus it is clear that it deals with terumah that is d'oraisa, and nevertheless if an olive's bulk is in the measure of eating a peras it is acceptable.
beur-hagra.4#ג: "That it is d'oraisa, etc." Chapter ha'Te'arovot (88b, 89a).
beur-hagra.4#ה: "If there were two, etc." Tosafot chapter 3 of Pesachim there, s.v. it challenged him, etc., and Or Zarua, etc. — thus in species not in its species a majority does not help when it is forbidden d'oraisa; and we establish that species not in its species is by taste d'oraisa, as written in chapter ha'Te'arovot (there); and the general matter is that we suspend only where it is permitted d'oraisa.
beur-hagra.5#א: "If there were two, etc." And it means where they do not combine — for example, two storerooms in two attics, as written in seif 7 and the like, as written in Yerushalmi chapter 4: You say baskets ascend and storerooms do not ascend — how is it done? Two storerooms in two attics and a se'ah of terumah fell into one of them — both are forbidden; and likewise regarding a mikveh in Tosefta of Mikvaot chapter 2, and the Rosh brought it, chapter 2: Two mikvaot that do not have forty se'ah and three log fell into one of them and it is not known into which it fell, and afterward rain fell and they were filled — Rabbi Yosi says they tell him not to immerse in either of them, etc., and on this.
beur-hagra.5#ב: "And even for d'rabbanan issur." From the mishnah, chapter 4 of Terumot, a litra of dried figs, etc., and all are forbidden, as written at the beginning of Yoma (4a).
beur-hagra.5#ג: "But if there is, etc." Tosefta there (chapter 6 of Terumot): In this one a hundred and in that one not a hundred — I say it fell into the one of a hundred; and there (chapter 2 of Mikvaot): One has forty se'ah and one does not have forty se'ah — I say they fell into the one of forty.
beur-hagra.6#א: "If there were here, etc." There and Yerushalmi chapter 4: Two baskets - in this forty se'ah and in that forty se'ah; a se'ah of terumah fell into one of them and it is known, etc., and afterward a second fell and it is not known into which - I can suspend and say to the place where the first fell, there the second fell. A se'ah of terumah fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and afterward a second fell and it is known into which - he cannot suspend and say to the place where the second fell, there the first fell. And likewise two mikvaot that do not have forty se'ah; three log fell into one of them and it is known into which they fell, and afterward two fell and it is not known into which - I can suspend and say to the place where the first fell, there the second fell. Three log fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and afterward two fell and it is known into which - he cannot suspend and say to the place where the second fell, there the first fell. And it deals with Rabbi Eliezer, seif 68, side 2, side 3.
beur-hagra.6#ב: "And specifically, etc." As above — we suspend only where it does not forbid, as written in that Tosefta and there chapter 6: And if it was tevel, etc. — they did not permit doubt, etc., as above; or where it is already forbidden, as written in chapter 6 there: One is mixed and one is not mixed — I say it fell into the mixed one; it specified that it is mixed. And likewise in Mikvaot there: One is drawn and one is not drawn — I say they fell into the drawn one; and many baraitot in chapter 6 of Terumot there.
beur-hagra.7#א: "If there were here, etc." Mishnah chapter 4 of Terumot: Two baskets and two storerooms, etc.
beur-hagra.7#ב: "And not only, etc." Tosefta chapter 6 and Yerushalmi chapter 4: Two baskets in two attics and two storerooms in one attic; and the Yerushalmi says there: But two storerooms in two attics — no. What is the difference between baskets and storerooms? Baskets are accustomed to be emptied, storerooms are not accustomed to be emptied. And Rabbi Shimon wrote there: According to this reason it applies when all six belong to another person who is accustomed to empty and mix — and now that which the Tosefta teaches, in this one a hundred and in that one not a hundred — I say it fell into the one of a hundred — what is the difference? Rather because of two people it was needed. And all this is that we suspend to be lenient in what is permitted from the Torah, as written in the earlier books; and likewise they said (there) in Yerushalmi on the baraita of Reish Lakish: He pressed in a circle, etc., s.v. they ascend, etc. — Rabbi Avin said one needs two litra in each, and all the more so enough to be nullified in the majority — meaning, with the litra; and even though it is d'rabbanan issur, one may say he holds like Rabbi Elazar in chapter ha'Areil (2a) that even for d'rabbanan a majority is required; and for Rabbi Yochanan two litra suffice; nevertheless for d'oraisa there must be permitted dry in dry by majority and species not in its species wet in wet by sixty — and here, species in its species by majority, as above.
beur-hagra.7#ג: "And some, etc." According to the Raah, that even species in its species wet in wet — no, only dry in dry, or d'rabbanan issurim and d'rabbanan measures; and therefore, s.k. 20.
beur-hagra.7#ד: "However, etc." In Yerushalmi there it does not appear so, for they say: Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Chiya in the name of Rabbi Shimon — before him were two baskets; in this fifty se'ah and in that fifty se'ah; a se'ah of terumah fell into one of them and he does not know into which — if he wished to separate from this he separates, from that he separates, half from this and half from that he separates; and likewise two mikvaot, etc. — thus it deals when they were not mixed, only to satisfy the stringent; since it is possible he satisfies even the stringent, and there is no concern of nullifying issur l'chatchila, for they combine when dry; but when wet it is that they do not combine, because he will taste it in eating or it is fit for noten taam; and since he mixes before eating it is permitted, as written in Yerushalmi chapter 4 of Terumot on the mishnah: Black figs elevate the white ones, etc., and it says he combines and permits; and likewise wheat — he grinds and permits.

kaf-hachayim.1#_: 1) [Seif 1] Two pots, one of heter and one of issur, etc.; if the piece is from d'rabbanan issur, etc. — a d'rabbanan doubt is ruled leniently. Shach, s.k. 1. Lechem HaPanim note 1, Shulchan Gavoah note 1, Beit Yitzchak vol. 1 in Amudei Zahav note 2; and accordingly for davar sheyesh lo matirin we do not say its doubt is lenient. Siftei Daat note 1, Arukh HaShulchan end of note 1; and see above siman 110, note 135.
kaf-hachayim.2#_: 2) There. Such as the fat of the gid; and cheese of a non-Jew and the like; even for issurim that have a Torah root — so the Rashba in Torat HaBayit HaArukh. Shach, s.k. 2. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot HaTur note 2, Peri Chadash note 1, Peri Toar note 1, Lechem HaPanim note 2, Binyamin Zeev note 1, Kereti note 1, Chavat Daat note 1, Shulchan Gavoah note 1, Beit Yitzchak vol. 1 note 1, Arukh HaShulchan note 5.
kaf-hachayim.3#_: 3) There. That we suspend judgment to say the issur fell into the issur, etc.; and the same if there were two pots, one of heter and one of issur, and before them two ladles — one of issur and one of heter — the law is likewise, for absorbed ben yomo is like the substance of issur for every law. Beit Yehudah note 1, Lechem HaPanim note 3, Binyamin Zeev note 2, Beit Yitzchak there in Amudei Zahav note 5, Zivchei Tzedek note 3.
kaf-hachayim.4#_: 4) There. And even if the heter in the pot is not greater, etc.; and it is possible that regarding stringent issurei mashahu we do not say "I say," even for d'rabbanan issurim with less than a majority — that is, until there is a majority of heter against the issur that fell in it. Nekudat HaKesef, chapter ha'Areil. Darkei Moshe note 1, Shach, s.k. 3. Knesset HaGedolah there note 3, Binyamin Zeev note 3; and he wrote that one may be stringent, unlike Peri Chadash note 2 who is lenient. And so too Peri Toar note 1, unlike Peri Chadash. Chavat Daat note 2, Zivchei Tzedek note 4.
kaf-hachayim.5#_: 5) And for davar sheyesh lo matirin — certainly we do not suspend. Kereti note 3, Arukh HaShulchan there; and see above siman 110 note 132 and in laws of double doubt, note 30.
kaf-hachayim.6#_: 6) And if there were two pots full of milk, one heter and one issur, and cold meat fell into one of them and remained overnight and was removed, and it is not known in which it was — it is permitted, for pickling is d'rabbanan and we say "I say"; nevertheless it is forbidden to boil the milk afterward; to eat it cold alone is permitted, for otherwise it would be a Torah issur and we would not say "I say" — what of that it was initially d'rabbanan. Siftei Daat note 3; and see above siman 87, note 12.
kaf-hachayim.7#_: 7) There. And the same law if there was only one pot of slaughtered meat and one of these two pieces fell into it, etc. It appears that here it deals with when the two pieces were recognizable by themselves before falling which was heter and which issur; but if they mixed first one with one, then since issur was established in both pieces each is judged as the substance of issur and we no longer say a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient. Shach, s.k. 4. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot HaTur note 5, Yeshuot Yaakov note 1, Chavat Daat note 3. However, Peri Chadash note 3 disagreed with the Shach and concluded that even when issur was established, a d'rabbanan doubt is lenient; and if so here in every case it deals whether the pieces were recognizable or not, and even though issur was established we suspend to be lenient — see there. And Peri Toar note 2 agreed; Peleti note 2; Kereti note 4; Lechem HaPanim note 5; Binyamin Zeev note 4; Siftei Daat note 4; and so Beit Meir in Kuntras Dinei Kavu'a, daf 38a, top of the page, on the Peri Chadash — the law is with him. And so Chacham Adam, klal 64, note 4: therefore, although regarding eating the pieces both are forbidden, nevertheless the pot is permitted and we establish the pot on its presumption — end. And therefore l'chatchila one should be concerned for the Shach and his colleagues, and in a case of loss one may be lenient.

kereti.1#_: The fat of the gid — even for issurim that have a Torah root, such as terumah that is d'rabbanan — Peri Chadash.
kereti.2#_: To say, etc. The Shach wrote in the name of Nemukei Yosef that for issurei mashahu we do not say "I say," and the Peri Chadash challenged; and see Peleti what he wrote on this; and I raised that regarding davar sheyesh lo matirin there is room for the Nekudat HaKesef's view.
kereti.3#_: Fell into the issur — even if it is an important item; Chayei Adam and so the later authorities; and see what Peleti wrote on this, that it is apparently against the Nekudat HaKesef's view.
kereti.4#_: And the heter, etc. The Shach wrote: nevertheless, when each is recognizable which is issur and which heter, and at the time of falling it was not known, etc.; but if the heter and issur pieces mixed first, issur was established and we do not say "I say." The Peri Chadash challenged on this that what he wrote — even when recognizable we call it established forbidden — see Peleti where I brought proof for the Peri Chadash from a complete mishnah in Terumot, see there.
kereti.5#_: It is not greater — for by Torah law we require a majority, for even if issur fell it is nullified in the majority; but for d'rabbanan, since a d'rabbanan doubt is lenient, we do not require an increase.
kereti.6#_: Also in this we suspend to be lenient — the Shach and the Peri Chadash agreed that the comparison is not exact: in the first case they were lenient even when issur was greater than heter, unlike the other cases where we require half-and-half; but if issur was greater we do not say "I say"; and see Peleti on this that even in the first case one may be stringent to require half-and-half.
kereti.7#_: But if issur was greater — see Peleti that the Raah holds that even here one may be lenient, and so inclines the Peri Toar. And I labored to reconcile what the Rashba challenged from the Talmudic sugya, see there.

mateh-yehonatan.1#_: (Siman 111 in Shulchan Aruch, seif 2) In what case is this stated, etc. — but if issur is greater than heter we do not suspend to be lenient. Later authorities challenge: do we not say in Pesachim daf 9b, two piles of matzah and one of chametz and before them two houses, etc. — that is two baskets as the mishnah teaches, see there in the sugya that compares bedikat chametz to two baskets; and so we rule in Orach Chaim siman 439, two piles, etc., that we say "I say," etc. — and it is not as the Mechaber writes here that issur must not be greater than heter; there, with piles and houses, it is apparently like issur greater than heter, for in any case one is liable for bedikah on that house — so why do we say "I say"? One may say: the reason issur must not be greater is so that issur not be established — for if issur is the majority, issur is established over heter; but if it is half-and-half, issur is not established more than heter, and we say "I say." And if so, there, since in any case this house has a presumption of heter, it is like half-and-half.
mateh-yehonatan.2#_: (There, seif 4) If the heter was greater, etc. — the two pots were of one species, etc. This law is from the Rashba in Torat HaBayit HaArukh; later authorities wondered at it, for he himself brought in Torat HaBayit, house 4, gate 1 [in the Berlin edition, daf 101b] that Rashi at the beginning of Chullin daf 95 holds that the Pesachim sugya deals with species in its species — otherwise the taste is like the essence of d'oraisa, and nevertheless it challenges from an olive in the measure of eating a peras that we should decree even in its species and not say "I say"; therefore the Gemara had to say it deals with terumah that is d'rabbanan, see there. And if so, it is necessarily clear that for d'oraisa issur, even in species in its species with a majority, we do not say "I say" — and if so the Rashba's words contradict each other. The Gaon Rabbi Eishel of Prague wished to resolve that the Rashba in Torat HaBayit did not decide whether we hold like Rashi that taste is d'oraisa or like Rabbeinu Tam that taste is not d'oraisa; if so, from doubt we rule stringently that taste is d'oraisa — and all this is in species not in its species itself; but our case is only a d'rabbanan decree of species because of not its species, and we say taste is not d'oraisa and for this it is a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient. One who examines the Rashba's words will see this resolution does not fit well, for the Rashba did not base the law here on taste not being d'oraisa. However, it appears to me to reconcile: it is apparently astonishing how one can say to decree because of not its species when everyone knows not its species is more severe than its species — for by Torah law one in two is nullified and not its species requires sixty; but regarding terumah, its species is more severe than not its species d'rabbanan, for by Torah law one in a hundred and not its species suffices by noten taam — and therefore it is fit to decree there species because of not its species; and therefore the Gemara challenges well that there, in terumah, it should not have said "I say," etc., and on this the Gemara answers it deals with terumah that is d'rabbanan; but for other issurim certainly the challenger did not think to decree species because of not its species — and the Rashba's words and the Mechaber stand.

mechaber.1#main: The law of pots of tereifah meat that became mixed with kosher ones. In it are 7 seifim: Two pots — one of heter and one of issur — and before him two pieces, one of heter and one of issur; if the piece is from a d'rabbanan issur, such as the fat of the gid hanasheh, and these fell into each other — they are permitted, for we suspend judgment to say the issur fell into the issur and the heter into the heter; and even if the heter in the pot is not greater than what is before him; and the same law applies if there was only one pot of slaughtered meat and one of these two pieces fell into it and it is not known which it is — we suspend judgment that the heter piece fell, even if the heter is not greater than the issur; or if there was only one piece of d'rabbanan issur and there are two pots, one of heter and one of issur, and it is not known into which it fell — in this too we suspend judgment to be lenient.
mechaber.2#main: In what case is this stated — that we suspend judgment in all these to be lenient even if the heter is not greater than the issur — when the issur is also not greater than the heter; but if the issur is greater than the heter we do not suspend judgment to be lenient.
mechaber.3#main: If the issur was from the Torah we do not suspend judgment to be lenient to say it fell into the issur until the heter is greater than the issur so that it will be nullified within it by Torah law.
mechaber.4#main: If the heter was greater than the issur so that it would be nullified within it by Torah law — we suspend judgment to be lenient. How so? Two pots — one of slaughtered meat and one of nevelah — and a piece of nevelah fell into one of them; if the heter in the pot of heter is slightly greater than the piece of nevelah we suspend judgment to be lenient, because by Torah law species in its species is nullified in the majority, except that the Sages required sixty. If the two pots were of one species and the issur of another species we do not suspend judgment to be lenient until the heter is sixty times the issur.
mechaber.5#main: If there were two pots of heter and before them two pieces, one of heter and one of issur, and one fell into this one and one into that one — both are forbidden, even in d'rabbanan issur, if neither has enough to nullify the issur; but if one of them has enough to nullify the issur — both are permitted.
mechaber.6#main: If there were two pots of heter and issur fell into one of them and it is known into which it fell, and again issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which — I say that to the place of the first issur the second also fell; but if issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and afterward issur fell into one of them and it is known into which — both are forbidden: {Rama: And specifically when there is not sixty to nullify the issur that fell there; but if there was sixty to nullify the issur that fell there it is as if no issur fell there at all (Beit Yosef in name of Rashba).}
mechaber.7#main: If there were two pots of heter and issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and one does not have enough to nullify the issur but both together have enough to nullify it — both combine to nullify it; and not only that but even one in the house and one in the attic combine; and the same law applies even for a hundred. In what case? When all belong to one person, for whatever belongs to one person will eventually become mixed; but if they belong to two people they do not combine: {Rama: And some are stringent that even for one person one may not be lenient; and for need of loss one may permit for one person; however one may not eat it except after they have been mixed together, for then the issur has already been nullified (Arukh general rule 26 in name of Maharish).}

peleti.1#א: Even if the heter in the pot is not greater — the Shach wrote in the name of Nemukei Yosef that he wrote, and these are his words: it is possible that regarding stringent issurei mashahu we do not say "I say," even for d'rabbanan issurim with less than an increase; but with an increase we say "I say," even for Torah issur. The Peri Chadash challenged: since issur mashahu is only d'rabbanan, it is proper to suspend to be lenient like other d'rabbanan issurim, for even though they were stringent about mashahu here they were not stringent. His words are correct in general; but if we analyze what issurei mashahu exist among d'rabbanan issurim, one almost finds only hard chametz which is d'rabbanan — nevertheless many authors forbid it in mashahu; and likewise tevel that is d'rabbanan, dough from which challah was not taken in the present era; and in these one may truly doubt, for that which we say we suspend without increase is because we rely on a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient — whereas tevel and chametz, the root of their issur is davar sheyesh lo matirin as is known; and in Beitzah, even though the issur is d'rabbanan, we say the doubt is stringent — and if so, perhaps also in these, where the doubt is stringent, we do not say we suspend without increase; requires study, investigate.
peleti.1#ב: And the same law, etc. — the Shach's view is specifically with two pieces, one issur and one heter, recognizable and standing by themselves, this issur and this heter; one fell and both are lost until it is unknown whether issur or heter fell. But if the pieces mixed before falling, issur spread through all of them one with one, issur was established, and whichever fell is as if issur fell. The Shach himself strained in the Perishah's intent and the Peri Chadash challenged that what he wrote — even when recognizable we call it established forbidden — whereas we concluded above that a d'rabbanan doubt is lenient. I wonder: is there not a complete mishnah in Terumot, chapter 7, mishnah 5 — two baskets, one terumah and one hullin, etc., and it is not known which is terumah and which hullin; if one ate from one he is exempt, etc.; one of them fell into hullin — it does not cause dimu'a, and the second is treated as terumah and liable for challah, and Rabbi Yosi exempts; a second fell elsewhere — it does not cause dimu'a; both fell in one place — it causes dimu'a, etc., end. And it is difficult: these se'ah are unknown which is terumah and which hullin — thus they were mixed and forbidden was established as the Shach wrote — so why do we not say "I say" regarding them? And if so, why when it fell into hullin does it not cause dimu'a — do we not say "I say" that it fell into hullin? Requires study. Yet one may understand: if so, even when they were mixed, when one fell into one of them we suspend to be lenient with "I say," etc.; and for d'rabbanan issur we do not require greatness, for for d'oraisa we require increase — and if so it is difficult what we teach: an idolatrous ring fell into ten thousand and from ten thousand into three — forbidden; why? Those thousands have one of issur and resemble two baskets of issur and one of heter mixed one with another, and when one fell elsewhere to three and the like — do we not say heter fell into heter? And if there is a majority of heter as we teach for three, even for d'oraisa we say so — and why mention that a ring is an important item, for the Shach and Peri Chadash raised that even for an important item we say "I say"? Requires study, apparently. Unless we say that they are never nullified even in thousands, even with "I say" we do not say regarding them — and if so, these are the things said in Nemukei Yosef that for issurei mashahu we do not say "I say."
peleti.1#ג: Also in this we suspend, etc. — the Shach and Peri Chadash stood that the comparison from those cases mentioned is not equal: in the first case there are two fallings of heter and issur; even if issur is greater than heter it helps. It appears to me that the Tur and Mechaber do not hold so; and although the Rashba said this, it is the reading he had from the Tosefta that caused him, for it teaches: two spice-measures, one hullin and one terumah, and he put from one of them and it is not known from which — I say from hullin he put, since it teaches stam "and he put" and did not specify inside the pot — we learn there is no insistence to put in whichever place he wishes, even a small vessel among small ones; and thus issur is greater and nevertheless we say "I say," and from this the Rashba learns his law. But from our reading that teaches two spice-measures and he put one of them into a pot and it is not known, etc. — thus it is customary that the pot is greater than putting spice from a spice-measure, and one may well say at least when issur is greater to be stringent, for there is no proof to be lenient. It is also possible to say the Rashba holds like Hagahot Asheri that the Shach brought above, siman 110: issur mixed in heter, even one in one, is permitted for two people — and thus here too he was lenient; but for us, who do not hold like the Rosh's hagahah, one may be stringent. And one should not challenge the Rosh's hagahah that for d'rabbanan one in one is nullified and a majority is not required — so why need "I say" regarding baskets to say certainly issur fell into heter, since it is half-and-half it is one in one and permitted? One may say: truly for all issurim one in one is permitted, but for terumah even a majority does not nullify terumah, and all the more so one in one; therefore "I say" was needed; investigate.
peleti.2#_: If issur is greater, etc. — this is the Rashba's view, that he holds like one version in Yevamot; but the Raah challenged and holds that even if issur is greater. Apparently the Raah has a decisive proof from Pesachim chapter 1: two baskets, one chametz and one matzah, and before them two houses, one checked and one not; a mouse came, took, and entered the houses — we say this is two baskets: chametz entered the unchecked, matzah entered the checked. It is difficult: is this not analogous to saying heter fell into heter — that issur does not exceed heter? If so, even issur into heter is half-and-half and we are lenient, unlike here with chametz: if chametz came into a checked house, behold all is issur and there is no heter against it — why do we permit it? See there in Pesachim; Tosafot also wrote: if it deals without nullification and it is d'oraisa it cannot be according to Rabbi Yochanan who requires increase — and if so this too is like it; requires study, apparently. Perhaps one may say: requiring that issur not be greater than heter is because then presumption of heter leaves the heter, for issur is greater upon it and it has presumption of issur; and this does not apply to houses, for a checked house certainly has presumption of heter. And further: therefore we require that issur not be greater than heter — when they are equal it is half-and-half, and one who eats from the pot into which the basket fell has two doubts: doubt that nothing fell from the issur at all, and if it fell, lest what he eats is the heter (see Tosafot Pesachim that all deals with dry in dry, see there, and see what I wrote above siman 109 at length). Unlike if a majority of issur fell — why say lest what he eats is heter? Behold issur is the majority and whatever separates from the majority is presumed separated, and he certainly eats issur — therefore it is forbidden, for on this "I say" they did not rely; without falling it is forbidden for he certainly eats what fell since it is the majority and from the majority we presume separation — therefore they were stringent, unlike regarding houses where this does not apply and a majority is not required; investigate.
peleti.4#_: If the heter was greater than the issur, etc. — this law requires study, especially regarding the Rashba, for we say in the Gemara two baskets, one hullin, etc. — we say hullin into hullin fell; and the Gemara challenges: according to the one who says an olive in the measure of eating a peras is d'oraisa, how do we say "I say"? And it answers: terumah that is d'rabbanan. Tosafot challenged in Chullin: it deals with its species and by Torah law it is nullified in the majority; and Rabbi Yochanan establishes it in Yevamot — that baraita when issur is greater upon heter; why need not its species without the measure of eating a peras — behold the taste is like the essence of d'oraisa; and necessarily in species not in its species; and Tosafot answer that thus the Gemara challenges: if you hold an olive in the measure of eating a peras is d'oraisa in not its species, even in its species the Sages should decree and forbid because of not its species, etc., end. And accordingly we who hold taste is d'oraisa must answer Tosafot's challenge as Tosafot say: if an olive in the measure of eating a peras is d'oraisa, even in its species one should decree, and on this the Gemara answers terumah that is d'rabbanan; for d'oraisa we decree. And if so, how does Shulchan Aruch explain for d'oraisa issur when there is a majority we say "I say" — for in not its species an olive in the measure of eating a peras is d'oraisa, even in its species one should decree; requires study. One may strain and say Shulchan Aruch chose another answer to Tosafot's challenge — "according to your reasoning," etc. But what shall we say of the Rashba who himself brought Tosafot's challenge and how can we say "I say" in d'oraisa doubt with a majority? Requires study. The great Rabbi my colleague Rabbi Shalom R"B resolved: when we need Tosafot's answer, it is if we hold taste is d'oraisa — then it is difficult to say in not its species that taste is d'oraisa, and it must deal with its species — and it is difficult, behold it is nullified in the majority, and one must say the majority does not help because of a decree because of not its species, etc.; but taste is not d'oraisa, and one may say it deals with not its species — then the challenge is well: an olive in the measure of eating a peras is d'oraisa, how are they nullified by the majority? Tosafot's answer is not needed. Behold this dispute of the rabbis whether taste is d'oraisa or not — the Rashba wrote: since it is Torah issur its law is to be stringent — meaning where there is no Torah issur we do not go to be stringent; if so, accordingly, when there is sixty, if taste is not d'oraisa there is no challenge, and necessarily from Tosafot's place it is proven one must decree regarding an olive in the measure of eating a peras, species because of not its species; but if taste is not d'oraisa there is no challenge, and if we are responsible for Tosafot's answer that one must decree, etc. — accordingly the view that one must decree is only a d'rabbanan decree, and for d'rabbanan we follow the lenient and say taste is not d'oraisa and we do not decree at all — and this is the Mechaber's intent; it requires further study, end of the words of Peh HaChochma Chen. It appears to me one should understand why in species in not its species it is not nullified in the majority and by Torah law it is nullified in the majority, and we do not decree in its species because of not its species — and necessarily one must say that here one cannot err, for everyone knows that by Torah law it is nullified in the majority, for there is its majority of heter and one of its species; but in not its species nullification in the majority does not apply since they are not one kind — and this is plain and necessary. Yet accordingly it is difficult how it can be thought to forbid in the measure of eating a peras in its species as a decree because of not its species — in not its species there is no nullification in the majority and we properly forbid an olive in the measure of eating a peras; but species in its species where there is a majority we do not say an olive in the measure of eating a peras, and in the majority itself it is not fit to say because of not its species as written, for regarding majority one cannot compare this to that or err — and apparently there is no place for Tosafot's answer, only for worldly issurim where truly by Torah law it is nullified in the majority and permitted to eat, and in not its species it is forbidden — so how can we decree an olive in the measure of eating a peras in its species because of not its species — this majority is forbidden and this permitted? But for Tosafot's answer in terumah, that even by Torah law it is not nullified in the majority and requires a hundred, and nevertheless for an olive in the measure of eating a peras they are lenient and say "I say" — one may fear even in not its species, err and be lenient; and one may say: this case is different, its species that is permitted in its majority and the difference is recognizable — for also in its species in its majority it is forbidden and requires a hundred, only because of "I say" they are lenient, fearing lest in not its species too one will be lenient; and the entire Tosafot answer speaks only of terumah, but for worldly issurim Tosafot's answer does not apply and there is no place to decree — and this is Shulchan Aruch's law; it requires further study, investigate well.
peleti.6#_: I say to the place of the first issur, etc. — he challenged: why need the place of the first issur — behold this pot is forbidden, and if so it is obvious we suspend the issur's falling into that pot. The Bach resolved: even for d'oraisa issur, where we do not say "I say," regarding this we say by force of this reasoning we suspend to the place where the first fell, etc.; and the later authorities challenged that this too is only a mere reasoning — Heaven forbid to rely on it in d'oraisa doubt — and they resolved because of the latter clause. The Shach resolved that here it is worse since it had presumption of heter only now that it fell — and this is strained. It appears to me the Mechaber, according to his view that we do not say chein nafsho for other issurim — one may say it deals with issur falling in a pot that had only the taste of olives established, and thus the pot is forbidden; afterward heter increased by two olives and the pot returned to heter (and it deals with wet in wet where squeezing out is not possible, forbidden); afterward another piece fell and it is unknown whether heter or issur — if we judge, since the pot is in presumption of issur, this piece too we establish in presumption of issur, for otherwise the pot is forbidden — that is, the pot is permitted because heter increased upon it and it returns to heter; but if we judge, since issur was established at the issur's falling, this pot too was established that issur fell there and the pot is forbidden — and what of that afterward they returned to heter? On this the Mechaber intended.
peleti.7#א: Combine — see Kereti who challenged that this is chein nafsho; see there what the later authorities resolved with difficulty; and see above beginning of siman 92. I find it difficult: why chein nafsho from here — we hold squeezing out is forbidden; if so, at least that pot is forbidden — how will the second pot help nullify? Therefore one may say: certainly if it were d'rabbanan issur all this would not be needed, for we say "I say" — all this is d'oraisa issur and therefore sixty is required; and chein nafsho, squeezing out — all is d'rabbanan, and if so the matter returns to "I say" and combination is not needed; it requires further study.
peleti.7#ב: And some permit — the later authorities stood on this from what is taught: two paths, one tamei and one tahor, and both went, one on this and one on that; we hold: if they come to ask one after the other, both are tahor and we suspend each on the tahor path he took — and if so here too with two people, if they come to ask one after the other we purify them and say to each that heter fell. The main challenge is below in laws of niddah regarding two women who found a stain on one garment — likewise the challenge. The main resolution, as written: with two paths, if one comes to ask a sage — I walked one path and do not know which — he need not mention that his fellow also went on one of the two paths; thus the sage asked only about him permits; and so for two. But here, if one comes to ask a sage about an issur piece that fell into a pot, the sage certainly forbids unless he mentions his fellow's pot too, that there are two pots and it is not known into which — and since he must mention his fellow's, it is as if asked about him and his fellow, and forbidden; investigate.

pitchei-teshuva.1#_: "The pieces." Avodat HaTaharah; and see Shaar HaMelekh chapter 10 of Hilchot Mikvaot, general rules of d'rabbanan doubt, rule 1 and rule 2 — he disagrees with the Peri Chadash on two points and with the Shach on one: that which the Peri Chadash wrote, that even when the pieces were recognizable by themselves it is called established issur — the main view appears like the Shach, that for d'rabbanan doubt we require full establishment of issur, etc.; and also that the Peri Chadash's view that even with presumption of issur we say d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient — the halachah is not so (and I already wrote this in laws of double doubt, note 21). But he also disagrees with the Shach: he wrote that even when the pieces are not recognizable, when issur was established we suspend to be lenient to say the heter piece fell — and specifically when d'rabbanan issur mixed one in one and afterward one was lost we do not say d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient since it was established; but when one fell into a pot of heter where there is presumption of heter against it — establishing the pot on presumption of heter — we suspend to be lenient, see there; and see responsum Toldot Yitzchak siman 420 what he wrote on this matter.
pitchei-teshuva.2#_: "We suspend to be lenient." See responsum Shemen Rokeach vol. 1, simanim 37, 38, and 39, who wrote that even if one of the pots is forbidden only by doubt, nevertheless we suspend regarding it; therefore he wrote in an incident that there stood three pots of heter and d'rabbanan issur fell into one of two of them, and in the third pot there was still no doubt; and afterward d'rabbanan issur fell into one of the pots and doubt arose in the third pot and on one of the first ones. The first two pots are certainly forbidden, as below, seif 5; and the third pot is permitted, for we suspend it on the two pots already forbidden — but if the first doubt was not known until after the second arose, one may reconcile the matter and in a case of great loss one may be lenient, see there. He also wrote that if the first doubt of those pots was not known until the second was known, then one may say somewhat that even the first of the first ones in which there is no doubt is permitted because of the second — but he did not have the heart to permit on this, see there for his reason.

rabbi-akiva-eiger-yd.1#_: (Siman 111, Taz, s.k. 5) That is, specifically in not its species. It is a stammer and missing language — for on the contrary, only in its species does it require a challenge.

siftei-kohen.1#א: ["From d'rabbanan issur. For a d'rabbanan doubt we rule leniently:"]
siftei-kohen.1#ב: ["Such as the fat of the gid. And cheese of a non-Jew and the like; even an issur that has a Torah root — so too the Rashba in Torat HaBayit:"]
siftei-kohen.1#ג: ["And even if the heter in the pot, etc. The Nekudat HaKesef, chapter ha'Areil, wrote that it is possible regarding stringent issurei mashahu we do not say \"I say,\" even for d'rabbanan issurim with less than a majority, end of his words; and he brings it in Darkei Moshe:"]
siftei-kohen.1#ד: ["And the same law, etc., from these two pieces, etc. It appears that here it deals with when the two pieces were recognizable by themselves before falling which was heter and which issur; but if they mixed first one with one, then since issur was established in both pieces each one is judged as the substance of issur itself and we no longer say a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, as written in the laws of double doubt, seif 41; and what the Perishah wrote, seif 62, that it deals with when the two pieces mixed first one with the other — applies explicitly to two pots, for even if we judge each one as the substance of issur itself, nevertheless there is a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient with two pots, unlike one pot; and investigate:"]
siftei-kohen.1#ה: ["And it is not known into which it fell, etc. Even if the pieces are worthy of honor, for by Torah law it too is nullified, but the Sages said a piece worthy of honor is not nullified; and in such doubt that one pot is nevelah they did not say so, end of Perishah, seif 64; and it appears to me the same applies to two pieces and two pots — the law is thus; and so the Nekudat HaKesef there: with two pots, one slaughtered and one nevelah, and before them a piece of nevelah and a piece of slaughtered meat that fell one into the other and it is not known into which they fell — by Torah law it is nullified in the majority, we suspend to be lenient since there is increase, and even for an important piece, for even a davar sheb'minyan by Torah law one in two is nullified, end of his words; and since he permits d'oraisa issur with increase, all the more so d'rabbanan issur itself; and it appears to me the same with two pieces and one pot — permitted even without one in one, for nevertheless we hold a d'rabbanan doubt is lenient; and on the contrary here we say more a d'rabbanan doubt than with two pots, as written below, s.k. 6, from Issur VeHeter, see there:"]
siftei-kohen.2#א: ["In what case is this stated that we suspend in all these, etc. All this is the Tur's language from Torat HaBayit; but it is difficult for me, for from the Rashba's words in Torat HaBayit it does not appear so, for he mentioned there only two pots; and afterward he wrote (daf 113, end of 1a), and these are his words: It is difficult regarding d'rabbanan issur — why need a majority for Reish Lakish, and even one in one for Rabbi Yochanan? For since we doubt whether terumah fell into hullin or not, it is a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient; and we learned in the Tosefta: Before him were two spice-measures, one hullin and one terumah, and he put from one of them and it is not known from which — I say from hullin he put — thus we always suspend to be lenient in their matters; and it appears to me that since terumah certainly fell here, only it is not known into which — not in this case is it a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, end of his words. Thus specifically with two pots, because issur certainly fell there, only it is not known into which — for Rabbi Yochanan one in one is required; but with two pieces and one pot it is possible that no issur fell into the pot at all — permitted even if issur pieces are greater than the pot, analogous to putting from two spice-measures and it is not known from which. And in the short Torat HaBayit (house 4, gate 2) he did not write this "in what case" that when issur is greater than heter we do not suspend so much to be lenient, only with two pots; and although he wrote there afterward: there were two pieces and one pot, etc. — permitted, "I say" the heter piece fell here, even though the heter in the pot is not greater than the piece that fell here, as we explained, end of his words. It appears the Tur took this from that he wrote "as we explained," and also from that he wrote "even though the heter is not greater than the piece," and he did not write "greater," and even though the heter is less than the piece — thus with two pots and two pieces in one pot the law is one; but one cannot say so, as proven in the long Torat HaBayit and as written — and the Tur did not see the long Torat HaBayit, as the later authorities wrote in several places; and also from his short words it appears so, for if he held one law for them he would have combined and taught them and should have arranged two pots and one pot all in one section as the Tur arranged, and he should not have interrupted there with many other laws — but since he interrupted the topic, we learn that with two pieces and one pot, even if the issur piece is greater than the pot, it is permitted; and what he wrote "as we explained" refers only to what he wrote before that for d'rabbanan we say "I say," and on this he says "as we explained" that we say "I say" for d'rabbanan; and that which he says "even though the heter is not greater," etc. — it is that even if the heter is less it is permitted, but he taught it thus because he must teach in the latter clause: if it is Torah issur we do not permit until heter exceeds issur. The Raah in Beit HaBechirah there disagrees with the Rashba and holds that even with two pots it is permitted even if issur is greater than heter, because of a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, see there:"]
siftei-kohen.2#ב: ["But if issur is greater, etc. One should not challenge: with one piece and two pots, where is it found that issur is greater than heter? If we know issur is the majority we examine the pot of heter — one may say it is found well when the issur was removed beforehand; and in Derishah he wrote in one answer, see there:"]
siftei-kohen.3#_: Until the heter is greater than the issur, etc. Meaning: in species in its species specifically a majority alone suffices, as below, seif 4.
siftei-kohen.4#א: ["If the two pots were of one species, etc. Not specifically — rather it comes to say that the pot of heter is not the species of the issur piece; and likewise if the issur pot is not the species of the heter pot and it is not known where it fell — it is a d'oraisa doubt."]
siftei-kohen.4#ב: ["The two pots, etc. And the same with one pot and two pieces when the issur piece is not the species of the pot — it is a d'oraisa doubt and stringent; and investigate."]
siftei-kohen.5#א: ["Forbidden — both of them. Because we do not say \"I say\" except where we suspend the issur into issur — we do not forbid the issur more than it already was; but here, where both are heter, if you suspend the issur in one and permit the second, behold you forbid one of them from its permissibility — and if so, since you forbid in any case one of them, on what basis did you forbid this one, lest the opposite — and therefore both are forbidden — so the Rashba in Torat HaBayit; and likewise we say below, siman 129, seif 43, and likewise regarding a stain, see there; and accordingly it appears explicitly that even with two pots of heter that are not equal but one small and one large, we cannot permit the large and say issur fell into the small — for in the end you forbid one of them from heter — on what basis, etc.; and the Rashba and those who follow him did not distinguish this at all, and so it appears to me, and not as Issur VeHeter, general rule 29, seif 5, who wrote we suspend to be lenient that it fell on the small one — see siman 151, seif 68, side 3:"]
siftei-kohen.5#ב: ["But if one of them has, etc. \"I say\" the issur fell into that one which has enough to nullify — Tur from Semak; and this is specifically d'rabbanan issur, but for d'oraisa we do not say \"I say,\" for d'oraisa doubt is stringent, as below, s.k. 14:"]
siftei-kohen.5#ג: ["Both permitted. And there is no distinction whether the two pots belong to one person or two people, end of Tur from Semak; and in the Arukh it is explained that he wrote so to exclude the Ramban, who holds that when belonging to two people and they come to ask one after the other, even if neither has enough to nullify we permit each one and suspend that it fell in his fellow's — see below, s.k. 19, the main view follows the Ramban. The Bach challenged: why do we not say the two pots combine to nullify when they belong to one person, as below, end of seif 7? The Shach resolved that here, since there are two pieces, it is worse; and so Maharshal in his hagahot to the Tur, and the Perishah brings it, seif 10 — and it is not reasonable to distinguish this also in the Rashba's words in Torat HaBayit, for it appears he makes no distinction here, only that here it does not deal with the law of \"I say\" but with combination he does not deal here at all; and it is possible here it deals with those cases in which combination below does not help, as written in s.k. 18; and so in Darkei Moshe; and in Derishah, seif 9, I again saw in Maharshal, Piskei HaGahot, siman 56, that he himself retracted his words and explained like the Shach, except that afterward he wrote at the end of the siman that for the law it is a sound reasoning that with two fallings they do not combine, see there — and this reasoning is weak; and so in Darkei Moshe that I brought below, s.k. 18, it appears explicitly that with two fallings they combine:"]
siftei-kohen.6#א: ["I say to the place of the first issur, etc. The Bach challenged: what does it teach? Is it not all the more so, for above, seif 1, with two pots, one heter and one issur, and one issur piece — we suspend that issur fell into issur, and all the more so here that we can say to the place where the first issur fell the second also fell? He resolved that here it teaches that even for d'oraisa issur we suspend to be lenient to say that to the place where the first issur fell the second also fell; and so in Issur VeHeter, general rule 26, seif 13, that all that is written in seif 5 and seif 6 — there is no distinction between d'rabbanan and d'oraisa issur, end of his words. I wonder: how can one say \"I say\" for d'oraisa? Behold an arranged Talmud, chapter 1 of Pesachim, daf 10, and all poskim agree we do not say \"I say\" for d'oraisa — and what of that issur fell first there? Every d'oraisa doubt is stringent. And further: why say in seif 4 for d'oraisa issur that fell where there is enough to nullify? I examined Issur VeHeter there and saw he did not write as the Bach, only after bringing seif 5 and seif 6 he wrote: it appears that in all this there is no distinction whether the issur is d'oraisa or d'rabbanan, end of his words. It appears he comes to say: it should not be, since the Rashba and those who follow him did not write that d'oraisa issur and d'rabbanan measure are like d'rabbanan issur, only with two pots of which one is issur — if so, specifically when one pot was already established as issur we say there is no distinction between d'rabbanan and d'oraisa issur and d'rabbanan measure such as species in its species by majority; but here the pots are heter — thus one should say specifically for issur that is purely d'rabbanan we suspend to be lenient, but not for d'oraisa issur and d'rabbanan measure; it teaches that this is not so — in all this there is no distinction between d'oraisa issur and d'rabbanan measure or d'rabbanan issur; and with this the Bach's challenge is resolved — why it should teach here that even though the pot was already established heter, only now at falling it deteriorated, nevertheless we suspend to be lenient; but for actual d'oraisa issur certainly we do not suspend to be lenient:"]
siftei-kohen.6#ב: ["Both forbidden. And we do not say that to the place where the last issur fell the first also fell; rather its law is as if issur fell and it is not known where it fell, as explained in seif 5, see there:"]
siftei-kohen.7#א: ["Both combine. And the same even for a hundred — whatever entered doubt because of issur combines to nullify it — Tur from Semak; and in the Arukh he wrote one resolution: specifically when neither alone has enough to nullify, only in both together; but if one has enough to nullify and the second does not, we do not say in this that it is permitted because it entered doubt — for that one which has enough to nullify did not enter doubt at all — for even if you say it fell inside, it is permitted except for the measure of \"I say\" in that which has enough to nullify it fell, end of his words; and the Beit Yosef brings it; and although he wrote there another resolution, nevertheless for the law both may stand; and also Darkei Moshe brought this resolution plainly, and I brought it in s.k. 18; and the Raah in Beit HaBechirah agreed to this resolution; and accordingly where \"I say\" does not apply, such as d'oraisa issur, it is forbidden; and even without this the Raah disagrees that two pots combine, as written in s.k. 20:"]
siftei-kohen.7#ב: ["Combine, etc. The Bach wrote that this is specifically according to the view that we do not say chein nafsho except for meat and milk and not for other issurim; but for us, who establish chein nafsho for all issurim, combination does not help even if the pots were mixed afterward unknowingly together, end of his words. It is difficult, for all the later authorities — Issur VeHeter end of general rule 26, Maharshal Piskei HaGahot siman 57, the Rav in Turei Zahav beginning of general rule 51, and the Magen Avraham — all copied the Rashba plainly that two pots combine; and it is strained to say the practical difference is when dry mixed with dry and neither alone has a majority but together they have a majority they combine, for with dry we do not say chein nafsho, as above siman 92, seif 4 in the gloss — for there it deals with two pots, that is, wet; and also strained to say that which the Rav rules here plainly like the Mechaber is according to what is written in siman 92 and in a case of great loss we do not say chein nafsho for wet — for if so why did the Rav bring here the view of those who are stringent, for without that one may not permit except in great loss; and further, Darkei Moshe wondered at the stringent and concluded: I do not know his reason, and if it is a received tradition we accept it; and if it is so, most poskim hold we say chein nafsho for wet, as the Rav wrote in siman 92. Rather it appears clear that even according to what we establish chein nafsho they combine, for we say chein nafsho only where it is known where it fell; but here where we do not know, everything that entered entered doubt and it will become mixed — we view it as already mixed, as the Tur wrote from Semak; and if so, since we view it as already mixed before the falling, it is as if it fell initially into the pot that has enough to nullify the issur — clear proof from the words of the Rav HaMagid, part 9 of Ma'achalot Assurot, law 9, as written in siman 92, s.k. 8, see there (and one may say according to what is written in siman 99, s.k. 15, that where nevelah, even though heter was added afterward before it was known, it is forbidden — that case is different, for afterward it became known where it fell, and thus at the time of falling not everything entered doubt, unlike here where it was never known where it fell, thus everything entered doubt; and investigate):"]
siftei-kohen.7#ג: ["Will become mixed, etc. The Magen Avraham wrote: it appears to me that even for one person, if it is known clearly that they will not become mixed — for example, one dish of milk and one of meat — they do not combine; and even if both are meat and one person will not eat them until he mixes them together, then the issur is nullified in its taste itself; however he may mix them l'chatchila and there is no nullifying issur l'chatchila here, for the issur is already nullified through combination, end of his words; and so in Darkei Moshe, as the Tur and Mechaber wrote in seif 5: but if one of them has enough to nullify, etc., and these are his words: it appears here it deals when the two pots are not one species and therefore they do not combine together to nullify; but when they are one species and stand to be mixed together, both combine to nullify the issur if they belong to one person. From the Rashba that the Beit Yosef brings, one may explain another resolution: we do not say that two pots combine to nullify except when both are in issur doubt, that is, when neither alone has enough to nullify the issur; but if one has enough to nullify we do not say they combine — so the Rashba resolved, end of his words; and from his words it appears that whatever are two species, even if permitted to mix them, as long as they are not accustomed to become mixed they do not combine; and so Maharshal, Piskei HaGahot, siman 56, and these are his words: the same applies to matters that do not stand to be mixed, even though all are one species — only that one was cooked with sweetness and one with sharpness in vinegar, or the like — they do not combine, end of his words; and it appears the Magen Avraham's view is likewise, and he mentioned meat and milk only as an example, and the same for anything known not to be accustomed to mix:"]
siftei-kohen.7#ד: ["Of two people, etc. The Bach wrote that the Rashba does not deal here except with d'oraisa issur, therefore he did not write to permit except for one person; but for d'rabbanan issur, although they do not combine, nevertheless we suspend to be lenient with two people when they come one after the other, end of his words. It is not so, and he did not examine Torat HaBayit (daf 113, 2b) where it is explained there that even for d'rabbanan issur we do not suspend to be lenient with two people who come one after the other with two pots of heter or more — because since you must in any case forbid one of them from heter, all are forbidden: on what basis did you forbid this one, lest the opposite — therefore all are forbidden, see there; and nevertheless the Rashba's words are weak; and presently the Ramban's words that the Rashba brought there: he explained that the case of a litra of dried figs deals when they belong to one person or two who come to ask in one house; but if they come one after the other we suspend to be lenient, and when there is one pot of issur, even if they come in one house we suspend to be lenient — end, for thus it is necessarily proven from chapter 1 of Pesachim (daf 10) and chapter ha'Ishah she'Nitarmelah (Ketubot daf 26) that even when both are heter we suspend to be lenient for d'rabbanan issur when they come one after the other, see there. And what the Rashba challenged on him — if so, he should have explained that mishnah of a litra of dried figs that it deals with one person or one house — it requires further study, for there it does not deal with suspending to be lenient at all, only with combination where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree whether lower ones elevate upper ones; and likewise what the Rashba further challenged from that two people do not combine since they will not mix — according to the Ramban, combination is not needed either, for there too it deals only with combination and not suspending to be lenient, and it deals when both came in one house — and all this is clear; and so they ruled in Hagahot Maimoniyot of Chullin that even two pots of heter we suspend to be lenient with two people one after the other for d'rabbanan issur, and the Bach ruled; and perhaps the Taz and other later authorities who copied the Rashba's words agree to this — that although the Tur also copied regarding two pots of heter and there is no distinction whether of one person or two, one may say it deals with d'oraisa issur; and so what they copied here that with two people they are forbidden appears to deal when they came in one house, as I explained:"]
siftei-kohen.7#ה: ["For need of loss. That is great loss, as written in siman 108, s.k. 12, see there; and so it appears in the law that one may not permit except in great loss, for the Raah in Bedek HaBayit (daf 113, 2b) disagrees with the Rashba on this, and these are his words: these leniencies of two baskets combining were not said except for d'rabbanan issurim or Torah issur with d'rabbanan measures, and likewise dry in dry where there is no taste, or wet where there is sixty (except terumah and the like whose measure is more than sixty); but where there is taste — certainly wherever it gives taste or is fit to give taste, such as wet in wet, species in its species, without sixty — we do not say these leniencies, even for d'rabbanan issurim; and this law was not mentioned in anything that sits to give taste, for taste is never nullified, or fit to impart taste even if there is no taste yet, such as species in its species; end of his words. And although Baal Mishmeret HaBayit wrote on him that there are many errors in his words and no order — it is known that Baal Mishmeret HaBayit is the Rashba who authored Torat HaBayit and he is interested in the matter, see there; and likewise the poskim wrote that specifically for orlah and terumah and the like we say the issur elevates the heter, but not for issur that has enough to impart taste, even species in its species, since it can impart taste against not its species and taste is not nullified — and I brought their words in siman 99, s.k. 20, see there:"]

turei-zahav.1#_: "Also in this we suspend to be lenient." The language implies that here there was more reason to be stringent, hence it had to say "also in this"; and in truth it is all the more so, as the Beit Yosef wrote that this case is all the more so — from the Rashba in Torat HaBayit HaArukh, because we did not see anything fall into heter; and in the Perishah he thought this all the more so that the Beit Yosef wrote is his own words and therefore challenged him and said it is not all the more so, and he entered strained matters and was not precise. It appears to me to reconcile one who further analyzed what he wrote afterward: but if issur is greater than heter we do not suspend to be lenient — "all the more so" — he challenged: what is his intent with the language "all the more so" that he used, and why did he not say we do not suspend to be lenient as he wrote afterward for Torah issur? It appears to me that in the Gemara, chapter ha'Areil (Yevamot daf 82), it challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a mikveh and answers: no, we do not take the majority; and if you wish, say "I say" there, for one may say "I say" — meaning, lest it fell into terumah and there is no issur at all; and everywhere we hold like the latter language. And here, in the latter language, one may explain two meanings: one — since one may say "I say," therefore there is room to be lenient even if only a minority of hullin remained, nevertheless it is permitted — and this is the Raah's view in Bedek HaBayit. It is also possible to say: in a mikveh a majority must remain, and here half suffices; and so Mishmeret HaBayit. Therefore the Rashba said here: if only a minority of heter remained — although one may explain thus, nevertheless we do not follow such leniency "all the more so," since the leniency is by mere suspension — for here there is leniency in half, unlike a mikveh. And one may say that which he wrote before, "also in this we suspend," intended: it should not be that in this case of only one falling and a pot of issur present, one might say in every case there is room to be lenient and the leniency is clear in this — and there is a difference from what we wrote afterward regarding not suspending so much to be lenient; therefore he said here "also in this we suspend to be lenient," meaning there is no clear leniency here, only by mere suspension; therefore also here we do not suspend so much to be lenient. And it appears one should challenge what is written in this siman that if there is doubt whether d'oraisa issur fell, it is permitted at a d'rabbanan measure — and this contradicts the rule in siman 66, seif 4, that here we do not rule leniently but it is like certain d'oraisa; it requires further study, for here the heter is by force of "I say," and we explicitly say in chapter ha'Areil that I cited nearby that every doubt in which one can say "I say" that no issur fell here is more lenient.
turei-zahav.2#_: "But if issur is greater, etc." One should not challenge: since one knows the measure of heter in the pot and the issur — if so, let us see whether the heter in the pot increased from what was certainly there, issur fell; one may say this knows clearly there was more issur, such as he heard from another — but he does not know how much heter there was itself, whether it was as much as the heter now or less, until with the issur that fell there it became so much. And in Derishah he explains this regarding two dry pieces — that is, he knows the measure of issur and not the measure of heter; and now he finds two pieces, one large and one small, and he knows at least the small one is not issur, and it is unknown whether the large is issur — automatically there is a majority of heter over issur, or the large is also heter and issur fell into the issur pot.
turei-zahav.4#א: "For Torah law, species in its species, etc." The same applies to species in its species and not its species — for we say that what is not its species is as if absent, and its species is greater and nullifies it, as stated in siman 98.
turei-zahav.4#ב: "The two pots were of one species." Not specifically — rather the issur is not the species of the heter.
turei-zahav.4#ג: "Until heter exceeds issur by sixty, etc." This deals with a piece worthy of honor, for d'rabbanan sixty does not help; nevertheless here in doubt they were lenient — so in the Rosh, end of chapter ha'Areil, and in Torat HaBayit HaArukh he wrote, and these are his words: even though the Sages required more than sixty, end of his words — meaning, sometimes they require a hundred to nullify, such as terumah — that is specifically in not its species, as in chapter 2 of Orlah.
turei-zahav.5#_: "If neither has enough, etc." It implies that if both have enough to nullify the issur it does not help — and it is difficult, for at the end of the siman we say that whatever belongs to one person we say it will become mixed, etc.. And one may say: here it deals with belonging to two people, for the Tur wrote here that there is no distinction whether of one person or two; and in the Perishah he wrote in the name of Rashal that here it is different because there are two fallings, one heter and one issur, and this is worse than below where there is only one falling — and so Maharach; and he strengthened this reasoning, and these are his words: thus it is proven from our master's words in Orach Chaim, laws of chametz, that he did not distinguish between two people and one person except regarding one pile of chametz and two checked houses, etc., and he did not write so regarding two piles, one chametz and one matzah, and two houses that he mentioned before — rather certainly, with two piles, since the mouse certainly put chametz in the checked house, we do not suspend to be lenient — until here his language; and he was not precise here, for two paths themselves are like two piles and two houses, for there is one tamei path and one tahor and two people went, one on each, and each purified himself, and even so we distinguish there between two people and one person. And further: there they are more lenient with two people than one person, and here at the end of the siman they are more stringent with two people — rather necessarily this topic does not apply here. And the distinction itself that I cited in the name of the great ones above, between two fallings and one falling, appears not to exist, for the Rashba in Torat HaBayit HaArukh wrote, and all the more so when there is only one issur piece that fell into one of them, there is room to suspend to be lenient and say it fell into issur, for we did not see anything fall into heter — until here his language implies one law for them, only that it is all the more so from the law of two fallings; and whence do we distinguish and say that with one issur and one heter there are two fallings and one falling equal, but regarding two of heter there is a distinction regarding combination? For abundance of the matter I bring another proof from Torat HaBayit HaArukh, daf 113, that brings there from chapter ha'Areil: two baskets, one hullin and one terumah, and before them two se'ah, one hullin and one terumah, and they fell one into the other — permitted, "I say" terumah into terumah, etc.; and they disagree there, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — Reish Lakish holds we require hullin in the se'ah to exceed terumah in the basket; Rabbi Yochanan holds even if hullin did not exceed terumah. The Rashba analyzed there: even though Rabbi Yochanan does not require increase, nevertheless we require hullin equal to terumah, but not if hullin are less than terumah. He challenged: why not be lenient even when hullin are less — what is different from that which we learned in Tosefta Terumot: two spice-measures, one hullin and one terumah, he put from one and it is not known from which — I say from hullin he put — thus we always suspend to be lenient in their matters? Meaning: there is no heter at all, only what he put from one of them; and it appears to me that since terumah certainly fell here, only it is not known into which — not in this case is it a d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient, end. And if there were a distinction between two fallings and one, he should not have challenged at all from two fallings to one falling, lest there also be a distinction between them — rather certainly there is no such distinction at all. And the essence: the Rashba there challenges Rabbeinu Shimon who distinguishes between two people and one person, as written here at the end of the siman — why was this distinction not mentioned in the Gemara, and on this he disagreed with him, only from stringency he did not wish to be lenient against Rabbeinu Shimon; and if there were a distinction between two fallings and one, he should also have challenged why he did not distinguish this. One who examines Torat HaBayit HaArukh will see the Rashba labored to explain all distinctions in this law — why did he not also explain this distinction to clarify whether there is a distinction between two fallings and one? Rather certainly it does not exist at all. Regarding the challenge above in the Tur and Rashba's words: one who examines the Rashba there in the order of his words will see there is no challenge at all — for initially he wrote there that the Ramban holds there is a distinction here with two baskets of hullin into which terumah fell, like the case of a litra of dried figs that he brings there, that nullification is required and we do not say d'rabbanan doubt to be lenient — when they belong to one person or two who come to ask in one house, but like two paths; but if they belong to two people, nullification is not required at all, even if in both there is only a minority of terumah, nevertheless permitted because each says it fell in his fellow's, like two paths. The Rashba disagrees there that even with two people there is no heter here except through nullification specifically; but if there is nothing to nullify and you wish to permit by saying on each pot that it did not fall there but in the other — that is not so; not to speak of one person, which is obvious, for in any case it is issur to him, but even with two people we do not say each suspends on his fellow, since if you suspend on him you forbid him because he lacks measure to nullify.
