On this he said: there is no distinction between one person, etc.; and that which he wrote in what case when neither has enough — he did not mean that in both there is enough to nullify, only that perhaps in both there is not enough to nullify; rather here it deals where in any case one does not have enough to nullify — in this there is no distinction between one and two, and forbidden. Regarding combination of two he adjoined this so that afterward he would write there is a distinction between one person and two regarding combination — and why did he write in the Arukh truth that combination of both helps with two pots of heter, and did not distinguish whether one has enough to nullify? Because there he wrote according to his view that combination helps even with two people, unlike Rabbeinu Shimon who distinguishes. But the short version was stringent like Rabbeinu Shimon, that with two people combination does not help; therefore he did not write the law of combination first and relied on what he would distinguish afterward between one person and two regarding combination. All these matters are plain — no challenge arises except for one who does not examine well and thinks that which the Tur wrote above, and there is no distinction whether the two pots belong to one person, etc., refers to that which he said that specifically in one of them there must be enough to nullify — this is not so; it does not deal above except with the matter that nullification is in any case required, unlike the Ramban, and it does not yet deal with combination; but he wrote his law afterward regarding combination, that there is a distinction between one person and two. That which the Rashba cited here his law with two fallings intends to teach that even with two "I say" we suspend to be lenient, even with two of heter; and he cites wherever "I say" applies, and teaches here that truly there is no distinction between two fallings and one falling, even with two pots of heter. And although afterward in the law "I say" to the place where the first fell the second also fell, he cited only one falling — there it is no difference except to suspend the second on the first; and in this there is no greater leniency in two than in one, for there we know where the first fell — therefore he also cited in the second time one falling, only that it is known into which the second fell. One may challenge how the Rashba in the Arukh rejected the Ramban's words above, that he holds no nullification is needed with two people one after the other, from that below, if they belong to two people nullification is required and even combination does not help — nevertheless it is difficult from what the Ramban brought as proof from two paths that are permitted one after the other, and what is different here that even with two people one after the other nullification is specifically required, and even with one falling like below. One must say the Rashba holds we do not learn from two paths, for there it is different because doubt of tumah in the public domain is lenient — therefore we follow leniency there; and this distinction is in Rabbeinu Shimon, chapter 7 of Terumot, regarding two "I say." But from that which we learn in chapter 7 of Terumot in the mishnah: if one ate from one he is exempt because perhaps they are hullin — and Rabbeinu Shimon brings there from Yerushalmi that Rabbi Yochanan challenges this that we should follow Rabbi Yehudah with two paths who exempts with two people one after the other — and he concludes that all agree one after the other — it appears there too the leniency of two paths regarding one after the other exists also for terumah; and if so, at least with one falling why not be lenient one after the other without nullification? And likewise Hagahot Maimoniyot of Chullin learns from Rabbi Yochanan's two paths that I cited with two pots of heter and issur fell into one — we follow leniency with two people one after the other. I saw Maharach also challenged that they do not combine with two people one after the other — what is different from two paths? — and he brings that Hagahot Mardakhai of Chullin and resolves, and these are his words: it is possible that specifically for d'rabbanan issur we suspend to be lenient when they come to ask one after the other, but for d'oraisa issur we do not suspend to be lenient, as proven in laws of chametz; and since the Rashba wrote these laws plainly, even for d'oraisa issur, therefore he did not write to permit except for one person, end of his words — and he was not precise here, as I will write shortly. It appears to me that for Rabbeinu Shimon one must say that with two people they do not combine to nullify when two people come to ask in one house — then there are two stringencies: one, nullification is required, and second, they do not combine; and for him everything is satisfactory: that litra of dried figs has both leniency and stringency — stringency that nullification is required, leniency that all vessels combine; it deals specifically with one person, but the Raah's view that even with two people one after the other nullification is required — we do not know how to answer what is different from two paths, for in Yerushalmi they make them correspond as I cited above; and investigate.
turei-zahav.6#_: "And it is known into which it fell — explained in Torat HaBayit, and this is its language: and it does not have enough to separate, and its minority is forbidden, etc., until here. One should not challenge: if so, behold it was already certainly forbidden, the one — and this is that which the beginning of the siman inquires, one pot heter and one issur, that we follow leniency; it appears it teaches here that even though there is no Torah issur here, for it is nullified in the majority, only that it was forbidden because of minority d'rabbanan without sixty — we feared not to suspend to issur here; it teaches us. And we find such reasoning in siman 129: if we suspend on blood of purification to save her friend — there is a dispute there in the Tur's words and Maharach wrote that in this law, even if d'oraisa issur fell, we suspend to be lenient, for all that is written here from two pots of heter and two pieces before them until the end of the siman — there is no distinction between d'oraisa and d'rabbanan issur; and so Issur VeHeter, general rule 26, seif 13, end of his words — and it is not correct at all, for it is proven in chapter ha'Areil (Yevamot daf 82) that for every d'oraisa issur we do not say "I say," and here all permissions are by force of "I say" to the place where the first issur fell, etc. And explicitly Torat HaBayit wrote initially: two pots, one heter and one issur, issur fell into one of them, etc., that issur must be nullified in the majority, and he adjoined: if two pots of heter, etc., I say to the place where the first issur fell the second also fell, from the reason we said, end of his words — behold he tied the reason of heter to what is above, and we require it be permitted from the Torah at least, whether in the issur itself that is only d'rabbanan or in the measure of its nullification that is permitted from the Torah even though the issur itself is from the Torah; and so in all that he cited until the end of the siman — Heaven forbid to be lenient here in d'oraisa issur and d'oraisa measure, such as not nullified in the majority. And another clear proof from siman 107 regarding eggs or fish that we are concerned lest they remained at the end, etc. — why do we not say as here that whatever entered doubt of issur all combines? Rather necessarily there it is species in not its species — the impure fish has another name than the pure fish — and therefore Torah sixty is required; and here we do not say leniency in the whole siman except where permitted from the Torah. And in Issur VeHeter end of general rule 26 he copied the Tur's words on these matters from the beginning of the siman until the law: I say to the place where the first fell, etc., and wrote on this: it appears that in all this there is no distinction whether issur is d'oraisa or d'rabbanan, end of his words — behold he included all laws of this siman; and his intent is that even d'rabbanan measure, as written, is itself before d'oraisa issur and heter greater than issur — and this is plain to the understanding.
turei-zahav.7#א: "Will become mixed. Accordingly it is plain that if the two types of heter are forbidden in mixtures — for example, one meat and one cheese — they do not combine to nullify it. Rashal wrote that if they are not standing to be mixed — for example, one was cooked with sweetness and the second with sharpness — they do not combine.
turei-zahav.7#ב: "And some are stringent that even for one person, etc." In Darkei Moshe likewise in the name of Issur VeHeter end of general rule 26 in the name of Maharish who wrote: we do not rule so; and so in general rule 12. Darkei Moshe wondered: why do we not establish thus, for there is no dispute on this; and below he will copy the words of Issur VeHeter. It appears to me astonishing at this ruling that whatever entered doubt combines to nullify it — why did he rule above in Shulchan Aruch, siman 105, seif 15: if it is not known whether he touched all of them, all are forbidden — why do we not say all combine to nullify? And for a similar reason he wrote in Issur VeHeter, general rule 12, seif 9, that we do not establish like this ruling of siman 14.
turei-zahav.7#ג: "Except after he mixes them." Derishah uPerishah wrote, and these are his words: however, in Issur VeHeter, general rule 26, Maharish responded that we do not rule so, even for one person; and even for one who would permit, one may not eat except after they mix together, for then the taste of issur is already nullified, end of his words. It appears to me astonishing at what he wrote that one who permits does not permit except after mixing — this is not so, for the Rashba permits, and he brings in Torat HaBayit HaArukh, daf 114, Yerushalmi: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Chiya in the name of Rabbi Shimon — before him two baskets, in this fifty se'ah and in that fifty se'ah; a se'ah of terumah fell into one and it is not known into which — if he wished to separate from this he separates, from that he separates, half from this and half from that he separates; and therefore if in one there were a hundred and in one fifty, I say they fell into the hundred — and from there he raises and not from the fifty, end, meaning for giving the kohen's portion one gives only from where terumah was nullified. And if you say there is no heter except after mixing — how is it fit to say he separates half from this and half from that? Behold they are already mixed and all became one; otherwise all is forbidden. And further: if there is no heter except after mixing, why did he use the language that both combine — combination is not applicable here since they are already one through mixing; therefore it appears plain that even if they were not mixed, since by Torah law it is permitted through nullification in the majority but d'rabbanan requires sixty, and since there is doubt into which it fell and both entered doubt — both combine to nullify and each is permitted by itself, since they will become mixed we view them as already mixed. And what Issur VeHeter wrote: even for one who permits — he did not intend the Rashba's view who permits here, rather: one should not rule thus for halachah to be lenient, and even one who wishes to permit for halachah should at least not permit except after mixing; but forever the Rashba's view is permitted even without mixing — that after mixing it is permitted even for two people, for one may say that with two people it is nevertheless forbidden l'chatchila to mix because of nullifying issur l'chatchila, as above siman 99, seif 5; and for one person it is permitted l'chatchila to mix — for if you say permitted l'chatchila to mix because we view it as already mixed, we too say that in truth they are permitted even without mixing, since we view them as already mixed. Rather necessarily in truth it is so, only he was stringent here to mix first — and this is also the Rama's intent here. I wrote all this because Maharach wrote that the permission here is only for those who hold chein nafsho applies only to meat and milk, as written in siman 92 and 99; but for us, who establish chein nafsho for all issurim, there is no permission — for what fell into one of them became nevelah — this does not appear at all, for since both entered doubt it is as if they were already in one vessel and afterward fell there, as we proved shortly — and this is a plain, clear matter: for even according to those who say chein nafsho for other issurim, nevertheless one does not nullify issur l'chatchila — and if so, since here we left that rule and say we nullify l'chatchila, it itself also helps for everyone regarding not calling it nevelah — so it appears clear and plain to the understanding.

yad-avraham.1#_: (Siman 111, Taz, s.k. 6) The Taz wrote that even for d'oraisa issur we suspend to be lenient one after the other. He brought proof from chapter 7 of Terumot: two baskets, one hullin and one terumah, and it is unknown which; if one ate from one he is exempt; another came and ate the second — exempt; and the Yerushalmi compares this to two paths one after the other; and he left in doubt the Rashba who forbids even with one falling one after the other. Likewise he challenged in Orach Chaim siman 439 on the Tur regarding a mouse that entered one of two houses and it is unknown which — he requires bedikah one after the other. In siman 69 of Hilchot Niddah, siman 129, he wrote on this that it is not necessary. It appears to me as the Magen Avraham wrote in chapter 19 of Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah: where doubt comes first whether both come from one cause — we are lenient one after the other; and so with chametz and falling of issur, unlike terumah and two paths. But what the Peri Megadim in Orach Chaim wrote to reject the Taz's proof from terumah — that it deals with terumah in the present era or terumat perot that is d'rabbanan — does not appear so, for Rabbi Yochanan establishes it in Yerushalmi according to Rabbi Yosi, who holds in Yevamot that terumah in the present era is d'oraisa; and also it does not deal with perot, as there it teaches the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah on challah that applies only to the five species. And the Rambam, chapter 10 of Hilchot Terumot, wrote the reason they are exempt: he removes from his fellow — it appears also for d'oraisa terumah, only that one should not learn from this to chametz, as the Magen Avraham wrote. However, in the Raavad's hasagot, chapter 2 of Hilchot Chametz, it is explained as the Taz wrote.
yad-avraham.2#_: (In Shach, s.k. 19) He challenged the Rashba who forbids d'rabbanan issur that fell into one of two pots, even belonging to two people, unknown which, when they come to ask one after the other — for Pesachim (daf 10) and Ketubot (daf 26) prove plainly that we suspend to be lenient one after the other with two people for d'rabbanan issur. It appears as the Kesef Mishneh wrote in chapter 2 of Hilchot Chametz uMatzah, law 11, in the Rambam's reason there: he need not check two houses a second time because it is a double doubt — on each one it is possible to say the mouse did not enter it but his fellow's; and if you say it entered his, perhaps he ate it. And in Ketubot regarding saffron, the Rosh also wrote it is a double doubt: perhaps it was hidden, and if not hidden, perhaps it did not become impure — see Keren Orah who wrote it is like doubt of entry, for which we are lenient in any case for d'rabbanan. Since we arrive at this, that in Pesachim and Ketubot there are two doubts — therefore it is more lenient than d'rabbanan issur. There is no contradiction from there to the Rashba's view — know that in Ketubot they are lenient even with two people, and likewise in that case in Pesachim according to the Rambam. In my work I expanded further on these matters: an incident occurred — eight meat pieces were salted on the table and three or four on the bench; after they were rinsed and mixed together, ten treif pieces were found among them; it is known that one was on the bench, only it is unknown whether the rest on the bench were also treif and the kosher ones were not salted with them at all or not — and I permitted it. For besides what I raised regarding doubt of salting in a responsum to siman 110 nearby, there is further room to permit from this siman [111, seif 4]: two pots, one heter and one issur, and a nevelah piece fell into one — we say it fell into issur; and although there the falling was known immediately, nevertheless if it was not known until the two pots were mixed while cold and chein nafsho was found among them and it is unknown into which pot it fell initially — we say it fell into the place of issur, and we suspend the piece found now in the spoiled one, as proven in siman 129, seif 61.
